historical_timeline.summary: Born Dorothy Ann Willis in Lakeview, near Waco, Texas.
Enters treatment for alcohol use and emerges sober.
Elected Texas state treasurer; keynote address at the 1988 Democratic National Convention; elected governor in 1990.
Falls and breaks her hand; a bone density test shows osteopenia, described as early osteoporosis.
Publishes I'm Not Slowing Down: Winning My Battle with Osteoporosis; reports that her bone density has stabilized.
Dies at home in Austin, six months after esophageal cancer was found.

claims.statement: Ann Richards was born Dorothy Ann Willis on September 1, 1933, in Lakeview, near Waco, Texas.

She was elected Texas state treasurer in 1982, gave the keynote address at the 1988 Democratic National Convention, was elected governor of Texas in 1990, and served one term after losing her bid for re-election in 1994.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used for the synthetic modern occupation (public speaker and adviser).

claims.statement: She spoke openly about her past heavy drinking ("I smoked like a chimney and drank like a fish"), entered treatment, and emerged sober; one biography dates the treatment to 1980 and describes it as successful.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own public account of alcohol use disorder and long recovery, and of past heavy smoking. Used for the synthetic problem of alcohol use disorder in sustained remission and for the former-smoker history; the quit date for tobacco is not documented.

claims.statement: She said publicly that her mother had osteoporosis, broke "her arm, her hip," and developed a hump, and that osteoporosis was not the cause of her mother's death but led to it.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own public account of her mother's illness. Used for the family history and the parental hip fracture entered in FRAX.

claims.statement: Because of her mother's fractures, she asked her doctor at an annual checkup to test her bone density.

She had a bone density test after falling and breaking her hand. CBS News (2003) and a publisher's summary date this to 1996, and CBS says she fell twice and broke her hand and her ankle; a Publishers Weekly review dates the hand fracture to 1994.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The hand fracture is consistent across sources; its year (1996 in two sources, 1994 in one) and the ankle fracture (one source) are not. The case uses a fall with a hand fracture the year before the index visit and records the ankle fracture as reported in one source.

claims.statement: The bone density test showed osteopenia, which CBS News and the publisher's summary call an early stage of osteoporosis; in other interviews she said she had osteoporosis or early osteoporosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The published label is low bone mass (osteopenia), described as early osteoporosis. No source gives her T-scores; the synthetic T-scores stay in the low bone mass range.

claims.statement: CBS News reported in 2003 that she had shrunk three-quarters of an inch; in a 2002 television interview she said "my neck bones were collapsing and I literally was shrinking."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Lay description of height loss; no source reports a vertebral fracture. Used only for the measured height loss of about 2 cm in the synthetic examination.

claims.statement: She took a prescription medicine, began weight-bearing exercise and weight training, and changed her diet; CBS News reported in 2003 that her bone density had stabilized, and that she was a spokesperson for the maker of the medicine she took.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her public account of treatment. The product is not named in this record, and the synthetic treatment is chosen by guideline and her synthetic data, not by her real treatment.

claims.statement: In 2003 she published I'm Not Slowing Down: Winning My Battle with Osteoporosis, written with Richard U. Levine, MD, to encourage women and men to ask their doctors for a bone density test.
She was found to have esophageal cancer in March 2006, received chemotherapy, and died at her home in Austin on September 13, 2006, at 73.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; after the true-frame episode and not used in it.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate bone health in a 63-year-old postmenopausal woman after a fall with a hand fracture: read the DXA T-scores precisely (low bone mass, not osteoporosis by T-score), calculate FRAX with her risk factors, and base the treatment decision on the guideline thresholds; complete a secondary-causes work-up and correct vitamin D before an antiresorptive; choose therapy strictly by guideline and her risk; add calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing and balance exercise, and falls prevention; set the DXA follow-up interval and the drug-holiday reassessment; and give recovery-oriented care for an alcohol use disorder in long remission, with a structured safety assessment, on the CMID osteoporosis schedule.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Richards returns four weeks after her intake visit. She takes vitamin D3 1971 units every day. She has added yogurt, cheese, and calcium-fortified orange juice, and her three-day food record shows about 1200 mg of calcium a day. She keeps walking and lifting weights and has had no falls. She did not collect the 24-hour urine sample before this visit because she was traveling for three weeks. She saw the endocrinologist this morning. Her balance and strength program with the physical therapist starts next week, and she has a routine dental examination booked next month. She has had no alcohol and no cravings.

She collected the 24-hour urine sample over the weekend, and the result came back this morning with her blood tests. She finished all 16 sessions of the balance and strength program four days ago and now does the home program three times a week. She has had no falls. She has had no alcohol. She has read about the infusion and asked about the flu-like reaction that can follow a first dose.

Fell from standing height last year and broke her hand; one account also describes a second fall with an ankle fracture. She was told after an earlier test that she had early bone loss; no report is available. Her mother had osteoporosis with arm and hip fractures. Former heavy smoker, quit more than fifteen years ago; alcohol use disorder in sustained remission for more than fifteen years. Height 164.0 cm, about 2 cm below her recalled tallest; BMI 24.5. DXA today: lumbar spine T-score -2.3, femoral neck -2.0, total hip -1.7. Lateral spine DXA: no vertebral fracture. FRAX with femoral neck BMD (previous fracture and parental hip fracture entered): 22 percent major osteoporotic, 3.6 percent hip. assessment.display: Low bone mass with high fracture risk
assessment.assessment: By T-score this is low bone mass, not osteoporosis: the lowest value is -2.3 at the lumbar spine, and none is -2.5 or lower. The phrase early osteoporosis has no defined meaning and should not be used. A hand fracture is not one of the fractures that establishes osteoporosis on its own (hip or vertebra, or in low bone mass a proximal humerus, pelvis, or distal forearm fracture), but it followed a fall from standing height, so it is correctly entered as a previous fracture in FRAX. With that and her mother's hip fracture, FRAX is 22 percent for a major osteoporotic fracture and 3.6 percent for hip fracture, above the thresholds of 20 and 3 percent. Treatment is indicated by the BHOF 1993 and Endocrine Society thresholds, and AACE 1991 would call this osteoporosis on clinical grounds. By AACE 1991 she is in the very-high-risk group because of a fall with injury and a fracture within about the past year; she does not meet the Endocrine Society very-high-risk criteria, which center on severe or multiple vertebral fractures

Zoledronic acid 5 mg once a year is a first-line choice in both the high-risk and very-high-risk groups of AACE 1991 and is an initial therapy in the Endocrine Society guideline, with proven reduction of hip, vertebral, and nonvertebral fractures. Once-yearly dosing suits her travel. Anabolic therapy was discussed; with no vertebral fracture and no T-score below -2.5 it is not needed first, and it remains the option if she fractures on treatment. An oral bisphosphonate is a reasonable alternative. A selective estrogen receptor modulator is not suitable, because it has not been shown to reduce hip fractures and her hip risk is above threshold. Before the first dose, 25-hydroxyvitamin D must be 30 ng/mL or more, calcium and eGFR must be normal (creatinine clearance 35 mL/min or more), and a routine dental examination should be done

Normal calcium, PTH, phosphate, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, kidney function, TSH, and blood count make hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia, thyroid excess, and myeloma unlikely. Vitamin D of 24 ng/mL is insufficient and is being corrected. The 24-hour urine calcium is still needed to exclude hypercalciuria before treatment. Celiac serology and protein electrophoresis are not needed without bowel symptoms, anemia, or an unexplained abnormal result
Falls cause most of her fracture risk outside the spine. Her tandem stance of 8 seconds shows impaired balance; a supervised balance and strength program is the most effective fall-prevention step

assessment.display: Alcohol use disorder in sustained remission
assessment.assessment: Heavy alcohol use and smoking harm bone; her long abstinence from both removes them as current risk factors, so neither is entered as current in FRAX. Remission also lowers her fall risk. No change to the drug plan; avoid sedating medicines

recommendations: Treat: zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously once a year, starting once 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 30 ng/mL or more, calcium and eGFR are normal, and a routine dental examination is done; recheck these at about three months
Collect the 24-hour urine calcium before the first dose
Acetaminophen for the aches and fever that can follow the first dose
Continue vitamin D3 1971 units daily and about 1200 mg of calcium a day, mostly from food
Supervised balance and strength program now, then a home program; weight-bearing exercise most days
Fasting morning CTX three months after the first dose to confirm response; calcium and creatinine before each yearly dose; 25-hydroxyvitamin D yearly
Repeat DXA of the spine and hip two years after starting, on the same scanner

After three yearly doses, recalculate FRAX and reassess: a drug holiday of up to three years is reasonable if she has had no new fracture or injurious fall and the femoral neck T-score is above -2.5; if she remains at very high risk, continue to six yearly doses
Height and fall-risk screen yearly, with repeat vertebral imaging if height falls 2 cm or more

provenance_review.notes: Recent-death rule: only what Richards made public (her book, interviews, and press coverage) and basic biographical facts are used. Her real T-scores were not found and are not used; her real medicine is not named, and no promotional claim is repeated. The fracture year conflict (1996 or 1994) is recorded.

safe_messaging_review.notes: Alcohol and tobacco claims are marked sensitive; recovery is described in person-first, non-stigmatizing language; the safety assessment records no current risk and gives the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; her later cancer and death are recorded as history only, without detail.
